title: Nehru Teaches His Daughter from Prison
text:
Jawaharlal Nehru, a leader of India's independence movement, spent long years in British prisons. His only child, Indira, grew up seeing him rarely. In 1928, when she was ten and at school in Mussoorie, he wrote her a series of letters about the history of the earth, early humans and the first civilizations, later published as Letters from a Father to His Daughter.

On 26 October 1930, Indira's thirteenth birthday, Nehru was in Naini Central Prison near Allahabad. He wrote to her that he could not send her a present from jail, so he would send her letters instead, things of the mind and spirit that prison walls could not stop. That letter began a long series. Over the next three years, in prison after prison, without a library and relying largely on his notes and memory, he wrote her nearly two hundred letters telling the story of the world: ancient China and India, Greece and Rome, the rise of Islam, Europe's revolutions, empires and the struggle of colonized peoples.

The letters were published in 1934 as Glimpses of World History, and the book became a classic in India. Indira went on to become India's first woman prime minister.
lesson: Distance does not end a parent's role. Even far away, we can teach, share what we love and stay present in a child's mind.
source: Jawaharlal Nehru, Glimpses of World History (1934); Letters from a Father to His Daughter (1929)
